instances.title: Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
instances.venue: Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems
instances.description: Peers use a tit-for-tat-like 'choking' algorithm: each peer uploads to (unchokes) the peers that give it the best download rates and chokes the rest, plus one rotating 'optimistic unchoke' every 30 s to discover better partners and bootstrap newcomers.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design paper; claims robustness to free riding)
instances.pathology: Later work (Piatek et al. 2007) shows strategic clients can exploit it

instances.title: Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?
instances.authors: Michael Piatek, Tomas Isdal, Thomas Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Arun Venkataramani
instances.venue: USENIX NSDI 2007 (4th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design & Implementation)
instances.description: Measurement and modeling of real BitTorrent swarms show that tit-for-tat choking leaves significant altruism (all peers regularly contribute upload that does not improve their own performance); the strategic BitTyrant client exploits this by allocating upload to peers with the best reciprocation per byte.
instances.evidence: Measurement + trace-parameterized model + live deployment: BitTyrant gives a median 70% performance gain for a 1 Mbit client on live Internet swarms; if applied universally, strategic clients can hurt average per-swarm performance
instances.pathology: Unconditional altruism of high-capacity peers subsidises strategic peers; incentive not robust to strategic manipulation

instances.title: The EigenTrust algorithm for reputation management in P2P networks
instances.description: Each peer receives a global trust value computed as the left principal eigenvector of normalised local trust ratings (based on past satisfactory downloads), with pre-trusted peers; peers then prefer downloading from high-trust peers.
instances.evidence: Simulations: reduces inauthentic downloads under various collusion threat models
instances.pathology: Relies on pre-trusted peers; vulnerable to Sybil identities without identity cost

instances.title: Robust incentive techniques for peer-to-peer networks
instances.description: Models P2P as a Generalized Prisoner's Dilemma and proposes a 'Reciprocative' decision function (cooperate with peers in proportion to their generosity, using private and shared history) plus defenses against whitewashing by treating strangers adaptively.
instances.evidence: Simulation: drives strategic users to nearly optimal cooperation levels
instances.pathology: Whitewashing (cheap new identities) and collusion undermine shared history

instances.title: Free riding on Gnutella
instances.description: Documents the absence of any contribution-enforcing mechanism in Gnutella and the resulting free riding: most users share no files and a small fraction serve most content (the baseline problem incentive mechanisms target).
instances.evidence: Measurement (24-h sample of Gnutella messages): almost 70% of users share no files; nearly 50% of all responses are returned by the top 1% of sharing hosts
instances.pathology: Free riding / tragedy of the digital commons in absence of mechanism

instances.title: Mitigating routing misbehavior in mobile ad hoc networks
instances.description: A 'watchdog' overhears whether next-hop nodes forward packets and flags misbehaving nodes; a 'pathrater' then routes around them.
instances.evidence: Simulation: +17% throughput with 40% misbehaving nodes, overhead 9%->17%
instances.pathology: Pathrater avoids misbehaving nodes but does not punish them (they still get service)

instances.title: Performance analysis of the CONFIDANT protocol
instances.description: CONFIDANT makes misbehaviour unattractive by detecting and isolating misbehaving nodes; trust and routing decisions use experienced, observed and reported (second-hand) forwarding behaviour, i.e. reputation plus exclusion.
instances.evidence: Simulation: DSR with CONFIDANT outperforms defenseless DSR under misbehaving nodes
instances.pathology: Second-hand reports open door to false accusations

instances.title: Sprite: a simple, cheat-proof, credit-based system for mobile ad-hoc networks
instances.authors: Sheng Zhong, Jiang Chen, Yang Richard Yang
instances.field_of_use: Mobile ad hoc network packet forwarding
instances.description: Nodes earn credit for forwarding others' messages (reported via receipts to a credit clearance service) and pay credit to send their own, making forwarding incentive-compatible without tamper-proof hardware.
instances.evidence: Formal model with proofs of cheat-proofness; prototype shows small overhead; simulations show nodes cooperate and forward unless resources are extremely low

instances.title: The Sybil Attack
instances.description: Shows that without a logically centralised identity-certifying authority, a single faulty entity can present multiple identities, defeating redundancy- and reputation-based mechanisms.
instances.evidence: Theoretical impossibility result
instances.pathology: Sybil identities undermine voting, reputation and quorum mechanisms

instances.title: The Social Cost of Cheap Pseudonyms
instances.description: When identities are free, misbehaving users can re-enter under new names; the paper analyses 'dues-paying' by newcomers (distrust or fees for new identities) and once-in-a-lifetime identifiers as ways to sustain cooperation.
instances.evidence: Game-theoretic: suboptimal newcomer mistreatment is an unavoidable cost of cheap pseudonyms
instances.pathology: Cost borne by honest newcomers

instances.title: The Byzantine Generals Problem
instances.authors: Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, Marshall Pease
instances.description: Loyal generals reach agreement despite traitors via message-exchange/majority-vote algorithms; agreement is possible with oral messages iff more than two-thirds are loyal (n >= 3m+1).
instances.evidence: Proofs of possibility/impossibility bounds
instances.pathology: Guarantees fail if faulty fraction exceeds bound

instances.title: Practical byzantine fault tolerance and proactive recovery
instances.description: PBFT replicates services across 3f+1 replicas, requiring quorums of 2f+1 matching messages before committing, with view changes to replace a faulty primary and proactive recovery to periodically restore replicas.
instances.evidence: Implementation: BFT library and Byzantine-fault-tolerant NFS (BFS) performs 2% faster to 24% slower than unreplicated production NFS; tolerates any number of faults over the lifetime if fewer than 1/3 of replicas fail within a window of vulnerability
instances.pathology: Safety breaks if more than f faulty; no attribution of blame

instances.title: BFT Protocol Forensics
instances.description: Formalises 'forensic support': when faults exceed the tolerance threshold and safety is violated, honest replicas can identify, with cryptographic integrity, as many culpable replicas as possible, enabling ex post accountability.
instances.evidence: Forensic support depends heavily on minor implementation details

instances.title: PeerReview: practical accountability for distributed systems
instances.authors: Andreas Haeberlen, Petr Kouznetsov, Peter Druschel
instances.field_of_use: Accountable distributed systems (NFS, P2P, overlay multicast)
instances.description: Each node keeps a tamper-evident log of its messages; witness nodes audit logs by deterministic replay against a reference implementation, producing verifiable evidence of faults so correct nodes can be exonerated and faulty ones exposed.
instances.evidence: Practical on three systems (network filesystem, P2P, overlay multicast)

instances.title: Leases: an efficient fault-tolerant mechanism for distributed file cache consistency
instances.description: A lease grants a holder rights (e.g., to cache data) for a bounded time; rights expire automatically unless renewed, so a failed or partitioned holder cannot block others indefinitely.
instances.evidence: Analytic/trace: short leases give consistency with small overhead

instances.title: CircuitBreaker
instances.description: Wraps a protected call in an object that monitors failures; once failures reach a threshold the breaker trips and further calls fail immediately, with periodic half-open trial calls to reset.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Handling Overload (Site Reliability Engineering, ch. 21)
instances.authors: Alejandro Forero Cuervo (Beyer et al. eds.)
instances.description: Per-customer quotas plus client-side 'adaptive throttling': each client tracks requests vs accepts over two minutes and locally rejects requests with a probability rising as the backend rejects more, so clients self-limit load.
instances.evidence: Operational experience: stabilises overloaded backends (descriptive)

instances.title: Resource Quotas
instances.description: ResourceQuota objects cap aggregate resource consumption per namespace; requests that would violate the quota are rejected with HTTP 403 Forbidden, so teams sharing a cluster cannot exhaust common capacity.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Congestion avoidance and control
instances.description: Introduced slow-start, additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease congestion avoidance and RTT-based retransmit timers so senders voluntarily reduce sending rate on packet loss, sharing capacity of a common network.
instances.evidence: Response to 1986 Internet congestion collapses; restored stable throughput
instances.pathology: Relies on voluntary compliance by end hosts

instances.title: TCP Congestion Control (RFC 5681)
instances.authors: M. Allman, V. Paxson, E. Blanton
instances.description: Standards-track specification requiring TCP senders to implement slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery, codifying cooperative back-off as an Internet norm.
instances.evidence: descriptive (standard)

instances.title: Congestion Control Principles (RFC 2914, BCP 41)
instances.description: Best Current Practice explaining why end-to-end congestion control is needed to prevent congestion collapse and ensure fairness among flows, and noting proposals for routers to detect and penalize flows not using acceptable congestion control.
instances.evidence: descriptive
instances.pathology: Non-responsive flows can free-ride on TCP back-off

instances.title: Promoting the use of end-to-end congestion control in the Internet
instances.description: Proposes router mechanisms to identify and restrict the bandwidth of high-bandwidth best-effort flows that are unresponsive or not TCP-friendly, creating an incentive for end-to-end congestion control.
instances.evidence: Analysis/position paper arguing router mechanisms are needed; discusses identifying flows as unresponsive, not TCP-friendly, or using disproportionate bandwidth (abstract checked)
instances.pathology: False identification of flows

instances.title: Analysis and simulation of a fair queueing algorithm
instances.authors: Alan Demers, Srinivasan Keshav, Scott Shenker
instances.description: Fair queueing gives each flow a separate queue served round-robin (bit-by-bit emulation), so ill-behaved sources cannot capture more than their fair share and well-behaved sources are protected.
instances.evidence: Analysis and simulation: fair allocation of bandwidth, lower delay for sources using less than their share, and protection from ill-behaved sources vs FCFS

instances.title: TCP congestion control with a misbehaving receiver
instances.description: Shows misbehaving receivers can drive senders arbitrarily fast (ACK division, DupACK spoofing, optimistic ACKing) and proposes protocol modifications (e.g. nonces) that make cheating detectable.
instances.evidence: Demonstrated attacks on real stacks; modifications eliminate the behaviour
instances.pathology: Cooperative protocols assume honest peers

instances.title: Additional HTTP Status Codes (RFC 6585)
instances.description: Defines 429 Too Many Requests, allowing a server to signal a client exceeded a rate limit, optionally with Retry-After telling it how long to wait.
instances.evidence: descriptive (standard)

instances.title: Rate limits for the REST API
instances.description: Primary per-user/app request quotas per hour plus secondary rate limits on concurrency and abusive patterns; exceeding them returns errors and continued requests while limited can lead to integration bans.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: An empirical study of spam traffic and the use of DNS black lists
instances.description: Measures SMTP traffic to MIT CSAIL (2000 and 2004 traces) and how local mail hosts query DNS blacklists (shared lists of spam-sending or open-relay IPs) to refuse mail from listed hosts.
instances.evidence: Measurement: email volume rose 866% from 2000 to 2004; DNSBL lookups were 14% of all DNS lookups at the border in 2004 (0.4% in 2000); 80% of identified spam sources were listed in some of seven popular DNSBLs
instances.pathology: Lists incomplete; false listings; spammers rotate IPs

instances.title: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) (RFC 7489)
instances.description: Domain owners publish policies (none, quarantine, reject) telling receivers how to treat mail failing SPF/DKIM alignment, plus aggregate reporting back to the domain owner.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Email sender guidelines
instances.description: Senders must authenticate (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), support one-click unsubscribe and keep user-reported spam rates in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%, else deliverability is degraded or mail rejected: a sender reputation threshold.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail
instances.description: Requires a sender to compute a moderately hard function (proof of work) per message, imposing a small cost that is negligible for normal users but prohibitive for bulk junk mail.
instances.evidence: Theoretical design
instances.pathology: Burdens low-power legitimate senders

instances.title: Programming semantics for multiprogrammed computations
instances.authors: Jack B. Dennis, Earl C. Van Horn
instances.description: Introduces capability lists (C-lists): a process can access an object only via an unforgeable capability it holds, so authority is explicitly granted and bounded.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: The protection of information in computer systems
instances.authors: Jerome H. Saltzer, Michael D. Schroeder
instances.description: Sets out design principles including least privilege, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation and separation of privilege (e.g. requiring two keys), limiting what any program or user can do and the damage from errors or abuse.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design principles)

instances.title: Efficient software-based fault isolation
instances.description: Software fault isolation rewrites untrusted code so its memory accesses and jumps are confined to its own fault domain, sandboxing modules within a single address space.
instances.evidence: Benchmarks: faster cross-domain communication than hardware isolation at the cost of slightly increased execution time for distrusted modules

instances.title: Certificate Transparency (RFC 6962)
instances.authors: B. Laurie, A. Langley, E. Kasper
instances.description: Certificate authorities submit certificates to public append-only Merkle-tree logs; monitors and auditors can detect misissued certificates and misbehaving logs, making CA misbehaviour publicly discoverable.
instances.evidence: descriptive (standard)

instances.title: Certificate transparency
instances.description: Explains CT as public, verifiable logs of all issued certificates so domain owners and third parties can spot rogue certificates, with browsers requiring proof of logging.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Internet X.509 PKI Certificate and CRL Profile (RFC 5280)
instances.description: Defines certificate revocation lists by which a CA publishes serial numbers of certificates revoked before expiry (e.g. key compromise), which relying parties check before trusting.
instances.evidence: descriptive (standard)
instances.pathology: Revocation checking is often soft-fail in practice (not from this source)

instances.title: Chrome's Plan to Distrust Symantec Certificates
instances.authors: Devon O'Brien, Ryan Sleevi, Andrew Whalley
instances.description: After misissuance incidents, Chrome announced a phased removal of trust in Symantec-issued certificates: a browser root program expelling a certificate authority.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow? Revisiting Eric Raymond with bug bounty programs
instances.description: Bug bounty programs pay security researchers for reported vulnerabilities; the paper analyses how reward levels drive discovery as vulnerabilities are progressively exhausted.
instances.evidence: Probability of finding additional bugs decays fast and can hardly be matched by increased rewards; researchers switch programs
instances.pathology: St-Petersburg-like diminishing returns; researcher churn

instances.title: An Empirical Analysis of Software Vendors' Patch Release Behavior: Impact of Vulnerability Disclosure
instances.description: Publication of vulnerability information (disclosure) acts as a threat that pressures vendors to patch.
instances.evidence: Disclosure raises instantaneous patch-release probability ~2.5x; open-source vendors patch faster

instances.title: Vulnerability Disclosure Policy (90+30)
instances.description: Vendors get a 90-day deadline to patch after notification; details are disclosed 30 days after the patch, or at the deadline if unpatched: a pre-announced deadline with publication as the sanction.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: The CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure
instances.description: Guidance on multi-party coordination among finders, vendors and coordinators, with a coordinator (CERT/CC) mediating embargoes and disclosure timelines.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure (security.txt, RFC 9116)
instances.description: Organisations publish /.well-known/security.txt with Contact and Policy fields telling researchers how to report vulnerabilities, lowering the cost of cooperative disclosure.
instances.evidence: descriptive (standard)

instances.title: Proof-of-stake rewards and penalties
instances.description: Slashable behaviours (double proposals, conflicting attestations) burn up to 1 ETH and force exit over 36 days, with a correlation penalty on day 18 scaled by how many validators were slashed around the same time; attestation rewards pay honest validators.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Proof-of-stake rewards and penalties: inactivity leak
instances.description: If the chain goes more than four epochs without finalising, an emergency 'inactivity leak' progressively drains stake from non-participating validators until participants again hold a 2/3 supermajority and finality recovers.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Casper the Friendly Finality Gadget
instances.description: PoS finality overlay with explicit slashing conditions; 'accountable safety' guarantees that conflicting finalized checkpoints imply at least 1/3 of stake provably violated a slashing condition and can be penalised.
instances.evidence: Proofs of accountable safety and plausible liveness

instances.title: Blockchain without Waste: Proof-of-Stake
instances.description: First formal economic model of proof-of-stake: because PoS validators must also be stakeholders, forking harms the value of their own coins, so a sufficiently modest reward schedule yields an equilibrium with immediate consensus and precludes persistent forking.
instances.evidence: Theoretical model (equilibrium analysis)

instances.title: Majority is not enough: Bitcoin mining is vulnerable
instances.description: Shows Bitcoin's block-reward mechanism is not incentive-compatible: colluding 'selfish miners' that withhold blocks earn more than their fair share, rational miners join them, and the group grows toward a majority; proposes a protocol modification.
instances.evidence: Analysis: unless assumptions on network propagation are made, selfish mining may be feasible for any coalition size; the proposed fix prohibits selfish mining by coalitions below 1/4 of resources (not the assumed 1/2)
instances.pathology: Reward mechanism rewards deviation; incentive to form pools

instances.title: Arbitrum: Scalable, private smart contracts
instances.authors: Harry Kalodner, Steven Goldfeder, Xiaoqi Chen, S. Matthew Weinberg, Edward W. Felten
instances.description: VM managers agree off-chain (unanimous assertions); a single manager may post a disputable assertion with a currency deposit, and any other manager can challenge within a timeout by posting a deposit, triggering an on-chain bisection protocol down to one instruction. The winner recovers its deposit plus half the loser's; the other half goes to the Verifier.
instances.evidence: Prototype: VM advanced at ~970,000 hashes/s vs ~1,600/s total for Ethereum; verifier handled over 5,000 disputable assertions per second

instances.title: Fault proofs explainer
instances.description: Permissionless fault proofs: anyone can propose output roots or challenge them via op-challenger during a ~7-day challenge period; proposals and challenges require escalating bonds held in DelayedWETH so they can be redirected to the correct party.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Chainlink 2.0: Next Steps in the Evolution of Decentralized Oracle Networks
instances.description: Oracle nodes post LINK deposits that are slashed (confiscated) on misbehaviour, with an alerting/escalation tier; staking gives nodes a financial incentive to report correctly.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design)

instances.title: Augur: a decentralized oracle and prediction market platform
instances.description: REP token holders stake tokens on observed outcomes and earn settlement fees; token holders can post progressively larger REP bonds to dispute outcomes, and past a threshold REP forks into outcome-specific versions, so only the version matching reality keeps value.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design whitepaper; abstract of current arXiv version checked)

instances.title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments
instances.description: Old channel states are invalidated by exchanging Breach Remedy Transactions; if a party broadcasts a revoked state, the counterparty can take all channel funds as a penalty.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design)
instances.pathology: Requires counterparty (or watchtower) to monitor chain

instances.title: Compound v2 Governance
instances.description: COMP token-holders govern via Governor Bravo proposals with voting delay, voting period, quorum and a Timelock that delays execution, plus a Pause Guardian.
instances.evidence: descriptive
instances.pathology: Token-weighted voting concentrates power in large holders (not from this source)

instances.title: Kleros: A Socio-Legal Case Study of Decentralized Justice & Blockchain Arbitration
instances.authors: Luis Bergolla, Karen Seif, Can Eken
instances.venue: Ohio State Journal on Dispute Resolution 37:55-98 (2022); SSRN preprint
instances.description: Socio-legal case study of Kleros, blockchain arbitration relying on smart contracts and crowdsourced, economically incentivized jurors; introduces the 'decentralized sheriff' (Kleros's crowd-based token-certification compliance mechanism) and analyzes obstacles to adoption.
instances.evidence: Case study plus exploratory observational user survey and interface trials
instances.pathology: Prior studies warn of risks to procedural safeguards from anonymous, economically incentivized jurors; adoption obstacles

instances.title: A Flexible Design for Funding Public Goods
instances.authors: Vitalik Buterin, Zoë Hitzig, E. Glen Weyl
instances.description: Quadratic finance: a matching fund tops up contributions so a project's funding equals the square of the sum of square roots of individual contributions, approximating optimal public-good provision.
instances.evidence: Theoretical: under the 'standard model' the mechanism yields first-best public goods provision; variations limit cost and help protect against collusion
instances.pathology: Vulnerable to collusion and Sybil contributions

instances.title: Community Guidelines strike basics on YouTube
instances.description: First violation is usually a warning that expires after 90 days (or after optional policy training); repeat violations within the window yield strikes with escalating restrictions and three strikes in 90 days terminate the channel; severe abuse can mean immediate termination; appeals possible.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Restricting accounts
instances.description: Strike ladder: first strike a warning, 2-6 strikes feature limits, 7 strikes a 1-day content-creation restriction, 8 three days, 9 seven days, 10+ 30 days; continued violation leads to account disabling; severe policies get extra restrictions.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: The Facebook Oversight Board: Creating an Independent Institution to Adjudicate Online Free Expression
instances.description: Documents creation of an independent, externally funded board hearing user appeals of Facebook content decisions with binding case decisions and policy recommendations.
instances.evidence: descriptive (participant-observation)
instances.pathology: Limited jurisdiction and capacity relative to decision volume

instances.title: "At the End of the Day Facebook Does What It Wants": How Users Experience Contesting Algorithmic Content Moderation
instances.authors: Kristen Vaccaro, Christian Sandvig, Karrie Karahalios
instances.description: Online experiment testing different appeal designs for contesting automated moderation decisions.
instances.evidence: None of the appeal designs improved perceived fairness, accountability, trust or control vs no-appeal baseline
instances.pathology: Appeals seen as ineffective/legitimacy gap

instances.title: Birdwatch: Crowd Wisdom and Bridging Algorithms can Inform Understanding and Reduce the Spread of Misinformation
instances.description: Crowd contributors write and rate notes on posts; a bridging (matrix factorization) algorithm shows notes only when rated helpful by raters who usually disagree, and contributors' rating ability is gated by their track record.
instances.evidence: Notes judged informative across political lines and reduced resharing of noted posts (per title/abstract)

instances.title: Community notes reduce engagement with and diffusion of false information online
instances.description: Examines the effect of crowd-sourced fact-checking notes attached to potentially misleading posts.
instances.evidence: Once a note is attached, posts receive significantly fewer reposts, likes, replies and views; diffusion paths change
instances.pathology: Notes often arrive after most spread (not from abstract)

instances.title: Trust among strangers in internet transactions: Empirical analysis of eBay's reputation system
instances.description: eBay's bilateral feedback forum lets buyers and sellers rate each other after transactions; cumulative scores are public.
instances.evidence: Empirical (1999 eBay data): feedback provided more than half the time despite free-riding incentives; almost always positive; reputation profiles predictive of future performance though eBay's net score is far from the best predictor; high buyer-seller feedback correlation suggests reciprocation and retaliation
instances.pathology: Reciprocal/retaliatory feedback skews ratings positive

instances.title: Reputation systems
instances.description: Reputation systems collect, distribute and aggregate feedback about participants' past behaviour so the shadow of the future constrains strangers' present behaviour.
instances.evidence: descriptive
instances.pathology: Under-provision of feedback, positive bias, cheap pseudonyms

instances.title: Engineering Trust: Reciprocity in the Production of Reputation Information
instances.authors: Gary Bolton, Ben Greiner, Axel Ockenfels
instances.description: Lab experiments on redesigning feedback information flow (e.g. blind/simultaneous or one-sided feedback) to curb reciprocity that distorts reputation information.
instances.evidence: Design changes yield more accurate reputation information, more trust and more efficient trade
instances.pathology: Reciprocity/retaliation in feedback

instances.title: Reciprocity and Unveiling in Two-Sided Reputation Systems: Evidence from an Experiment on Airbnb
instances.authors: Andrey Fradkin, Elena Grewal, David Holtz
instances.description: Field experiment hiding each party's review until both submitted (simultaneous reveal).
instances.evidence: More reviewing, less retaliation and reciprocation, lower ratings; no reduced adverse selection

instances.title: A first look at online reputation on Airbnb, where every stay is above average
instances.authors: Georgios Zervas, Davide Proserpio, John W. Byers
instances.description: Compares Airbnb and TripAdvisor ratings of the same properties to assess the informativeness of platform ratings.
instances.evidence: Nearly 95% of Airbnb properties average 4.5 or 5 stars and virtually none below 3.5; TripAdvisor hotels and B&Bs average 3.8 and 4.1 stars; ~85% of TripAdvisor vacation rentals at 4.5+; among cross-listed properties 14% more are rated 4.5+ on Airbnb, with weak cross-platform correlation
instances.pathology: Rating inflation reduces informativeness

instances.title: You Can't Stay Here: The Efficacy of Reddit's 2015 Ban Examined Through Hate Speech
instances.description: Reddit banned r/fatpeoplehate and r/CoonTown for harassment-policy violations: collective removal of a community.
instances.evidence: More accounts than expected left; those staying cut hate speech by at least 80%; receiving subreddits saw no increase
instances.pathology: Possible migration off-platform

instances.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Deplatforming as a Moderation Strategy on Twitter
instances.description: Permanent bans of high-profile influencers (Alex Jones, Milo Yiannopoulos, Owen Benjamin).
instances.evidence: Reduced conversation about them; supporters' activity and toxicity declined
instances.pathology: Migration to alternative platforms

instances.title: Does Transparency in Moderation Really Matter? User Behavior After Content Removal Explanations on Reddit
instances.authors: Shagun Jhaver, Amy Bruckman, Eric Gilbert
instances.description: Moderators providing removal explanations that educate users about community norms.
instances.evidence: Explanations reduce odds of future post removals

instances.title: The Internet's Hidden Rules: An Empirical Study of Reddit Norm Violations at Micro, Meso, and Macro Scales
instances.description: Analyses moderator-removed comments to map community norms at macro (site-wide), meso (shared by groups of subreddits) and micro (community-specific) levels.
instances.evidence: 2.8M comments removed by moderators of 100 top subreddits over 10 months; computational + qualitative analysis identified macro, meso, and micro norms

instances.title: Shaping Pro and Anti-Social Behavior on Twitch Through Moderation and Example-Setting
instances.authors: Joseph Seering, Robert Kraut, Laura Dabbish
instances.description: Compares positive example-setting (imitation) with moderation tools: proactive chat modes restricting content and reactive bans/timeouts.
instances.evidence: Users imitated observed behaviour, more from high-status users; proactive chat modes effectively discouraged spam

instances.title: Slash(dot) and burn: distributed moderation in a large online conversation space
instances.description: Randomly selected users with good karma receive limited moderation points to rate comments, and meta-moderators rate the moderations, distributing moderation across the community.
instances.evidence: Distributed moderation works in qualified way (timeliness, accuracy challenges)
instances.pathology: Slow moderation; unfair moderations

instances.title: STFU NOOB! Predicting crowdsourced decisions on toxic behavior in online games
instances.description: The Tribunal is a two-stage crowdsourced system: players report toxic players, and peer reviewers vote on aggregated reports to decide punishment; paper trains classifiers to predict these decisions.
instances.evidence: 10M+ reports on 1.46M cases; crowd decisions predictable by ML
instances.pathology: High human cost and time

instances.title: Wikipedia:Blocking policy
instances.description: Administrators block accounts to protect the project; blocks are preventive not punitive and 'may escalate in duration if problems recur', and can be appealed.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Wikipedia:Edit warring (three-revert rule)
instances.description: The three-revert rule forbids more than three reverts on a single page within 24 hours; gaming just outside the window still counts as edit warring, and violations lead to blocks.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Wikipedia:Arbitration Committee
instances.description: An elected panel of volunteer editors that imposes binding solutions to serious conduct disputes the community has been unable to resolve, and controls access to CheckUser/Oversight permissions.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Scaling Consensus: Increasing Decentralization in Wikipedia Governance
instances.description: Interview study of English Wikipedia showing governance becoming increasingly decentralized as the community grows, for both content decisions and social structures regulating behaviour, as predicted by commons-governance theory (Ostrom).
instances.evidence: Qualitative: in-depth interviews with 11 Wikipedians holding a variety of roles

instances.title: The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System: How Wikipedia's Reaction to Popularity Is Causing Its Decline
instances.description: Examines quality-control mechanisms (reverts, algorithmic rejection tools, formal rules) introduced to manage growth.
instances.evidence: Restrictive quality control and algorithmic rejection tools implicated in declining newcomer retention
instances.pathology: Sanctioning apparatus drives away good-faith newcomers

instances.title: Privileges
instances.description: Privileges control what users can do; users gain moderation and editing privileges (e.g. trusted user at 20,000, site analytics at 25,000) by earning reputation from peers' votes.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Steering user behavior with badges
instances.authors: Ashton Anderson, Daniel Huttenlocher, Jon Kleinberg, Jure Leskovec
instances.description: Formal model and Stack Overflow data on badges as incentives that steer users toward targeted actions.
instances.evidence: Formal model + Stack Overflow data: badges steer behaviour consistent with model predictions, e.g., users increase targeted activity as they approach a badge boundary; different badges produce different amounts of steering

instances.title: Code of conduct in open source projects
instances.authors: Parastou Tourani, Bram Adams, Alexander Serebrenik
instances.description: Empirical study of codes of conduct adopted by open-source projects, their content (e.g. derived from Contributor Covenant) and enforcement provisions.
instances.evidence: Mixed quantitative/qualitative study with practitioner interviews: top codes of conduct are adopted by hundreds to thousands of projects and share 5 common dimensions

instances.title: Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct v2.1
instances.description: Enforcement guidelines ladder: 1 Correction (private warning), 2 Warning, 3 Temporary Ban, 4 Permanent Ban, applied by community leaders according to impact.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Linux Kernel Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct Interpretation
instances.description: Interpretation of the adopted code of conduct: maintainers handle issues, the Technical Advisory Board (TAB) receives violation reports, and a conflict mediator is available.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Apache Voting Process
instances.description: Code modifications require consensus approval where a negative vote by a PMC member is a binding veto (with justification); other decisions use majority or lazy consensus.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: Developer Certificate of Origin 1.1
instances.description: Contributors sign off each commit certifying they have the right to submit it under the project's license, creating an attributable ex ante commitment.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: The Emergence of Governance in an Open Source Community
instances.description: Multimethod study of one open-source community (Debian) finding that members developed a shared basis of formal authority but limited it with democratic mechanisms that allowed experimentation with shifting conceptions of authority; the settled conception was more expansive than the original design.
instances.evidence: Multimethod: qualitative study plus statistical test of predictors of leadership

instances.title: Limiting interactions in your repository
instances.description: Maintainers can temporarily restrict activity (e.g. to prior contributors or collaborators, or blocking accounts under 24 hours old) for 24 hours to 6 months to cool down heated discussions.
instances.evidence: descriptive

instances.title: On the Formal Specification of Electronic Institutions
instances.description: Electronic institutions specify roles, dialogical scenes, performative structures and normative rules so that agents' interactions are constrained to institutionally permitted moves.
instances.evidence: descriptive (formal specification)

instances.title: On social laws for artificial agent societies: off-line design
instances.description: Designers impose social laws that restrict agents' available actions off-line so that agents can pursue goals without conflict; the paper studies the computational complexity of designing useful laws.
instances.evidence: Complexity results (NP-completeness)

instances.title: Introduction to normative multiagent systems
instances.authors: Guido Boella, Leendert van der Torre, Harko Verhagen
instances.description: Normative MAS are systems in which norms (obligations, permissions, prohibitions) and their violation, detection and sanctioning are explicitly represented and agents can reason about them.
instances.evidence: descriptive (special-issue introduction defining normative MAS)

instances.title: An integrated trust and reputation model for open multi-agent systems
instances.authors: Trung Dong Huynh, Nicholas R. Jennings, Nigel R. Shadbolt
instances.description: FIRE integrates interaction trust, role-based trust, witness reputation and certified reputation (agent-presented references) to estimate trustworthiness of partners.
instances.evidence: Empirical evaluation (simulation): FIRE helps agents gain better utility by selecting appropriate partners than benchmarks under various conditions

instances.title: REGRET: reputation in gregarious societies
instances.description: ReGreT combines individual (direct), social (witness, neighbourhood) and ontological dimensions of reputation, using social network structure to weigh information.
instances.evidence: descriptive model with initial experiments on the benefit of a social view of reputation (checked in the workshop version 'REGRET: A reputation model for gregarious societies')

instances.title: Trust in multi-agent systems
instances.authors: Sarvapali D. Ramchurn, Dong Huynh, Nicholas R. Jennings
instances.description: Survey distinguishing individual-level trust (learning, reputation, socio-cognitive) from system-level trust mechanisms (protocols making lying irrational, reputation mechanisms, security).
instances.evidence: Survey

instances.title: A survey of trust and reputation systems for online service provision
instances.authors: Audun Jøsang, Roslan Ismail, Colin Boyd
instances.description: Survey of trust and reputation computation (summation, Bayesian, discrete, belief, fuzzy, flow models) and centralized vs distributed architectures.
instances.evidence: Survey
instances.pathology: Unfair ratings, change of identities, discrimination

instances.title: Leveled Commitment Contracts and Strategic Breach
instances.description: Leveled commitment contracts set the level of commitment by breach penalties: an agent can be freed from the contract by paying a pre-specified decommitment penalty to the other party.
instances.evidence: Game-theoretic analysis: agents breach strategically (reluctant because the other party might breach first), yet leveled commitment increases both parties' expected payoff and enables deals impossible under full commitment
instances.pathology: Strategic under-breaching

instances.title: Kleros Short Paper v1.0.7
instances.authors: Clément Lesaege, Federico Ast, William George
instances.description: Jurors self-select into subcourts by staking PNK tokens and are drawn with probability proportional to stake (anti-Sybil); they commit-then-reveal votes, jurors coherent with the final ruling earn arbitration fees and take part of the stake of incoherent jurors (a SchellingCoin-style focal point on honesty), and appeals require fees plus an extra stake compensating the winner of frivolous appeals.
instances.evidence: descriptive (design whitepaper with worked examples)
instances.pathology: Coherence-based rewards reward agreement with the majority rather than correctness per se

instances.title: Market-Based Multirobot Coordination: A Survey and Analysis
instances.authors: M. Bernardine Dias, Robert Zlot, Nidhi Kalra, Anthony Stentz
instances.description: Survey of market-based multirobot coordination, in which robots bid for tasks in auctions using cost/revenue estimates so that allocation emerges from local, price-mediated negotiation; applied from mapping and exploration to robot soccer.
instances.evidence: Survey

instances.title: Sold!: Auction methods for multirobot coordination
instances.authors: Brian P. Gerkey, Maja J. Matarić
instances.venue: IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation 18(5):758-768
instances.description: MURDOCH, an auction-based dynamic task allocation system (a Contract Net Protocol variant on a resource-centric publish/subscribe model), allocates tasks among failure-prone robots to approximate a global optimum of resource usage.
instances.evidence: Physical-robot validation in a tightly coupled manipulation task and a loosely coupled long-term autonomy experiment

instances.title: Consensus-Based Decentralized Auctions for Robust Task Allocation
instances.authors: Han-Lim Choi, Luc Brunet, Jonathan P. How
instances.description: CBAA and CBBA combine market-based task selection (agents bid on tasks) with a local-communication consensus routine on winning bids to resolve conflicts without a central auctioneer.
instances.evidence: Proofs of convergence to conflict-free assignment with worst-case performance guarantees; numerical experiments show better convergence and performance than existing auction algorithms

instances.title: Blockchain Technology Secures Robot Swarms: A Comparison of Consensus Protocols and Their Resilience to Byzantine Robots
instances.authors: Volker Strobel, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer, Marco Dorigo
instances.description: Robots in a swarm are controlled via blockchain smart contracts acting as 'meta-controllers', so collective decisions reach consensus despite malfunctioning or malicious (Byzantine) robots and resist Sybil identity forging.
instances.evidence: Simulation (robot swarm simulator) comparing against classical consensus protocols in a collective-sensing task

instances.title: Robot swarms neutralize harmful Byzantine robots using a blockchain-based token economy
instances.authors: Volker Strobel, Alexandre Pacheco, Marco Dorigo
instances.description: Robots hold crypto tokens required to take part in security-critical swarm activities; a smart contract redistributes tokens according to contributions so Byzantine robots soon run out of tokens and can no longer influence the swarm.
instances.evidence: Experiments with up to 24 physical robots and more than 100 simulated robots: the token economy neutralized Byzantine robots in collective sensing

instances.title: Adaptive Inter-Robot Trust for Robust Multi-Robot Sensor Coverage
instances.venue: Robotics Research (ISRR 2013), Springer Tracts in Advanced Robotics, pp. 167-183
instances.description: Robots adapt inter-robot trust weightings online from relative sensing performance: robots with better sensors take charge of larger regions and poorly performing robots have their regions reduced.
instances.evidence: Lyapunov-type proof that robots converge to locally optimal positions as good as if sensor qualities were known beforehand

instances.title: Resilient Flocking for Mobile Robot Teams
instances.authors: Kelsey Saulnier, David Saldaña, Amanda Prorok, George J. Pappas, Vijay Kumar
instances.description: Resilient consensus on direction of motion despite noncooperative (defective or malicious) robots: dynamic connectivity management keeps the communication network above a critical robustness threshold so consensus stays within the cooperative robots' initial values.
instances.evidence: Theoretical guarantee plus simulations with holonomic mobile robots

notes: Verification: DOIs confirmed via Crossref metadata (title/venue/year/first author); RFC DOIs follow the standard 10.17487/RFCnnnn pattern and RFC pages were opened. located_via='search' marks entries where the source's existence was confirmed but the specific claim/evidence was partly from abstract-only or memory, not the full text: Piatek 2007 and Kalodner 2018 (USENIX pages blocked by Cloudflare; metadata unverified beyond URL), Adar 2000 and Jung 2004 and Eyal 2018 and Resnick 2002 and Zervas 2021 and Anderson 2013 (quantitative figures from memory, flagged in evidence), Kleros (SSRN case study; juror-incentive details from general knowledge), Castro 2002, Saleh 2021, Buterin 2019, Floyd 1999, Demers 1989, Wahbe 1993, Zhong 2003, MAS papers (FIRE, ReGreT, Ramchurn, Josang, Boella, Sandholm), Forte 2008, O'Mahony 2007, Tourani 2017, Chandrasekharan 2018. Web search budget was exhausted before this run, so discovery relied on recall + Crossref/doc verification; no Kleros whitepaper PDF was reachable (kleros.io paths 404). Multiple entries share a single URL (ethereum.org slashing vs inactivity leak) intentionally as separate mechanisms. Candidate mechanisms missing from sensitizing list: challenge period / fraud-proof with bonded challengers (optimistic rollups, Lightning breach remedy, Arbitrum); accountable safety / forensic attribution (Casper, BFT forensics, PeerReview); quorum/supermajority thresholds (BFT); leases / time-bounded grants; capability-based access & least privilege; sandboxing/fault isolation; circuit breaker / self-throttling (adaptive throttling, TCP back-off as voluntary restraint); fair queueing / per-flow isolation; resource quotas; privilege ladders earned by reputation (Stack Overflow); blind/simultaneous-reveal feedback (Airbnb, eBay redesign); bridging-based crowd annotation (Community Notes); meta-moderation (Slashdot); disclosure deadlines as threat (Project Zero 90+30); bug bounties; sender authentication/policy publishing (DMARC); proof-of-work/pricing via processing; identity cost / anti-Sybil newcomer dues; removal explanations (norm education); proactive content restrictions (Twitch chat modes); interaction cool-down limits (GitHub); timelocks on governance execution; decommitment penalties (leveled commitment); root-program distrust of CAs (expulsion of intermediaries); social laws (ex ante action restriction). 2026-09-29 resume (web search): opened sources for 27 of the 28 located_via='search' instances (full text or publisher/API abstract) and set them to 'opened page'; huynh2006fire stays 'search' (confirmed only via search-result abstract snippets, Springer page redirected to login). Piatek 2007 and Kalodner 2018 verified from the author/USENIX PDFs (full author lists, venues, BitTyrant median 70% gain, Arbitrum deposit/bisection and split of the loser's deposit). All '(from memory)' numbers were checked: Adar ~70%/top 1%~50% confirmed; Jung & Sit corrected (866% email growth, DNSBL lookups 14% of DNS lookups, 80% of spam sources listed); Eyal & Sirer corrected (fix threshold 1/4; any coalition size absent assumptions); Resnick & Zeckhauser 2002, Zervas 2021 (95% at 4.5+ stars), Anderson 2013 replaced with source figures. Descriptions revised for Saleh 2021, Augur (dispute bonds and forking), Forte 2008, O'Mahony 2007, Sandholm 2001, Bergolla 2022 (venue OSJDR 37:55-98). Added the Kleros Short Paper v1.0.7 (lesaege2019kleros) as primary source and seven multi-robot/swarm instances (Dias 2006, Gerkey & Mataric 2002, Choi 2009 CBBA, Strobel 2020, Strobel 2023, Pierson & Schwager 2016, Saulnier 2017); DOIs checked on Crossref/OpenAlex.
